questions.q: what was about to happen?
points: within a few days the war would be decided / fought out at sea
a sea battle was coming

questions.q: explain in your own words why Hannibal had to fight by trickery.
points: he could not match the enemy in strength / weapons
so cunning / a stratagem was the only way to make up for this
he was outnumbered (in ships)

questions.q: why do you think Nepos mentions this detail?
points: the pots are cheap, ordinary clay
they would shatter when they landed
the homely detail makes the secret weapon all the more surprising
the pots hide what is inside them

questions.q: describe Hannibal’s preparations and the orders he gave his marines.
points: as many as possible
live venomous snakes
were to be collected
and put into earthenware pots
he collected a great number of them
on the very day of the sea battle
he called his marines together
all were to attack the one ship of King Eumenes
against the other ships they were only to defend themselves

questions.lemma: die ipso, quo facturus erat navale proelium
questions.q: why is the timing of Hannibal’s briefing important?
points: ipso: it was the very day of the battle
the plan was kept secret until the last moment
so the enemy could not learn of it
it raises the tension for the reader

questions.q: what further promise did Hannibal make to his men?
points: he would make sure they knew
which ship the king was sailing on

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal do we get, and how does Nepos create it?
points: he wants Eumenes out of the battle whatever it takes: aut cepissent aut interfecissent, either outcome will do
he knows how to motivate his men with a reward
hyperbaton of magno … praemio stresses the size of the reward
the chapter ends on the men’s incentive, so the reader expects a determined attack

questions.q: of which kingdom was Eumenes king?
points: Pergamum (in north-west Asia Minor)

questions.q: how does Nepos convey Hannibal’s confidence here?
points: facile: he tells his men they will manage it easily
serpentium multitudine: he trusts in the sheer number of snakes
indirect speech reports his orders briskly, as a commander sure of his plan

questions.q: what happened once Hannibal had encouraged his men?
points: the fleets of both sides
were led out
into battle

questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal did before the battle, and why.
points: once the battle lines were drawn up
before the signal for battle was given
he sent a messenger
in a small boat
carrying a herald’s staff
to show his own side
where Eumenes was

questions.q: how does this clause add to the tension?
points: it holds the fighting back
Hannibal’s trick takes place in the tense moment before the battle
the reader waits for the signal that has not yet been given

questions.lemma: ut palam faceret suis, quo loco Eumenes esset
questions.q: what was the real purpose of the messenger’s mission?
points: to make clear to his own side
where Eumenes was / which ship was the king’s
(the reader is told this before the enemy can guess it)

questions.q: why was the letter so important to Hannibal’s plan?
points: it was the bait
it got the messenger taken to the king
so it revealed which ship was the king’s
it looked like an offer of peace

questions.q: what happened after the messenger had been taken to Eumenes?
points: he pointed out the commander’s ship
to his own side
he returned to where he had come from
Eumenes opened the letter
he found nothing in it
except things meant to mock him

questions.q: what impression of Eumenes do we get, and how does Nepos create it?
points: he is humiliated: the letter holds only things ad irridendum eum
he is baffled: mirabatur neque reperiebat
he is rash: he joins battle statim
non dubitavit makes him seem bold, but the reader knows he is heading into a trap
at marks the turn from the messenger’s success to the king’s confusion

questions.lemma: nihil in ea repperit, nisi quae ad irridendum eum pertinerent
questions.q: what does this tell us about Hannibal?
points: he humiliates the king even before the battle
he shows contempt for Rome’s ally
he is confident / has a sense of humour
the letter itself was only a means of finding the king

questions.q: how does Nepos make the messenger seem harmless?
points: scapha: he comes in a tiny boat
caduceo: a herald’s staff marked him as sacred / an official envoy
so no one suspected him

questions.q: who were the Bithynians?
points: the subjects / people of King Prusias, from Bithynia (in north-west Asia Minor)

questions.q: how does Nepos show that the plan was working?
points: Hannibalis praecepto: they act on Hannibal’s orders
universi: every ship attacks together
they attack exactly the target he named, Eumenes’ ship

questions.q: explain in your own words how close Eumenes came to disaster.
points: he would not have reached safety
unless he had taken refuge
inside his own defences / garrison
on the nearby shore

questions.q: describe how the rest of the Pergamene fleet was defeated.
points: they were pressing their opponents hard
suddenly
clay pots were thrown onto their ships
at first they laughed
they could not understand why this was being done
they saw their ships filled with snakes
they were terrified by this new kind of attack
they could not see which danger to avoid most
they turned their ships round
they went back to their naval camp

questions.q: why do you think Nepos includes this remark?
points: it reminds the reader of the pots in the previous chapter
the reader knows what is inside them while the Pergamenes do not
it creates dramatic irony / suspense

questions.lemma: quae iacta initio risum pugnantibus concitarunt
questions.q: how does Nepos make this moment ironic?
points: the Pergamenes laugh at clay pots as weapons
the reader knows the pots hold snakes
initio (‘at first’) signals that the mood is about to change

questions.lemma: cum, quid potissimum vitarent, non viderent
questions.q: explain in your own words the problem the Pergamene sailors faced.
points: they could not decide / see
which danger they should most avoid
with snakes on board and the enemy all round

questions.lemma: puppes verterunt seque ad sua castra nautica rettulerunt
questions.q: what did the Pergamene ships do?
points: they turned their ships round / fled
they went back to their own naval camp

questions.q: how does this phrase link the end of the episode to the beginning of the Life?
points: prudentia recalls chapter 1, where Hannibal surpassed all other generals in prudentia
so the episode confirms Nepos’ first judgement of him
it shows the same skill on land as at sea

questions.q: what events were taking place in Asia at this time?
points: Hannibal’s war on behalf of Prusias against Eumenes / the sea battle against Pergamum

questions.q: why do you think Nepos stresses chance here?
points: Hannibal’s downfall begins with a careless remark at a dinner
it does not come from a defeat in battle
it makes his end seem unlucky / tragic
it contrasts with the deliberate hunt for him later (non fortuito)

questions.q: what does this phrase show about the Romans’ attitude to Hannibal?
points: they think Rome is not safe as long as he is alive
it shows the fear he still inspires
even though he is now an old exile
it is a striking tribute to him

questions.q: how does this phrase recall the beginning of the Life?
points: the superlative sums up the Roman view of Hannibal as their worst enemy
it recalls his lifelong hatred of Rome in chapter 1
and the oath he swore as a boy
the hatred runs both ways

questions.q: explain in your own words how Prusias tried to keep his own hands clean.
points: he refused to do himself anything against the laws of hospitality
he told the Romans to arrest Hannibal themselves
if they could
he told them they would easily find where he was

questions.q: what impression of Prusias do we get from his appeal to the laws of hospitality?
points: he keeps to the letter of hospitality
while betraying its spirit
he still tells the Romans where to find Hannibal
he is weak / hypocritical

questions.q: why is the word facile ironic here?
points: it echoes Hannibal’s own confident facile before the sea battle (chapter 10)
now the word is used against him
the hunter has become the hunted

questions.q: how does Nepos make the scene vivid here?
points: the scene is seen through the eyes of a slave boy
looking out from the doorway
the small, personal detail brings the reader into Hannibal’s house
the boy notices more armed men than usual

questions.q: describe what happened from the arrival of the Roman envoys to Hannibal’s orders to the boy.
points: the Roman envoys arrived
they surrounded his house
with a large number of men
a boy looking out from the door
told Hannibal that more armed men than usual were appearing
Hannibal ordered him to go round all the doors of the building
and report back quickly
whether he was surrounded on every side in the same way

questions.lemma: sensit id non fortuito factum, sed se peti
questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal realised.
points: this had not happened by chance
he himself was the target / was being hunted

questions.q: what does this tell us about Hannibal’s reason for taking poison?
points: he did not want to lose his life at someone else’s will
he wanted to keep control / die on his own terms
he would not be captured by the Romans

questions.lemma: venenum, quod semper secum habere consuerat
questions.q: what does this detail suggest about Hannibal?
points: he always kept poison with him
he had long expected such a moment
he was prepared / showed foresight
like the exits he built into his fortress

questions.q: how does Nepos sum up Hannibal’s life in this phrase?
points: his life was full of hardships
of many different kinds
the pair of adjectives sums up the eventful life told in the earlier chapters
perfunctus: he endured them to the end

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise Hannibal’s great age?
points: hyperbaton: anno is separated from septuagesimo
by the verb acquievit
so his age is the last word of the sentence
questions.guidance: Accept any two. Do not penalise a candidate who notes that Nepos’ figure is too high.

questions.q: what does Nepos say here, and how does it change the tone?
points: there is no agreement
about the consuls in whose year he died
the story ends and Nepos turns from praise to a plain discussion of his sources

questions.q: who was Polybius?
points: a Greek historian who wrote a history of Rome’s rise to power (including the war with Hannibal)

questions.q: what does this list of sources show about Nepos as a writer?
points: he takes care with his sources
he names three authorities
each gives a different date
he does not choose between them / leaves the question open
he cites his friend Atticus first and names his work

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a confident and resourceful commander?
points: he faces a clear disadvantage, outnumbered in ships and weaker in arms
he turns at once to cunning, which Nepos presents as a necessity
he devises a strange new weapon: live venomous snakes in clay pots
he prepares on a large scale, collecting as many snakes as possible
he keeps the plan secret until the very day of the battle
his orders are simple and clear: every ship against Eumenes, mere defence against the rest
he is sure the snakes will make it easy and promises a great reward

essays.lemma: imperavit quam plurimas … quo loco Eumenes esset
essays.q: how does Nepos build up suspense as the sea battle approaches?
points: the strange order to collect live venomous snakes makes the reader wonder how they will be used
the snakes are packed into ordinary clay pots, so their purpose stays hidden
the plan is revealed to the marines only on the day of the battle
the orders focus everything on one target, King Eumenes
Hannibal promises to show his men where the king is, without saying how
the reward for capturing or killing Eumenes raises the stakes
the fleets are drawn up, and the battle is held back while Hannibal sends his messenger

essays.q: how does Nepos contrast Hannibal and Eumenes?
points: Hannibal is in control from the start, acting before the signal for battle
he uses a messenger with a herald’s staff to find out where Eumenes is
Eumenes’ side is easily fooled, sure that the letter is about peace
the messenger returns safely with his mission done
Hannibal mocks Eumenes with an insulting letter, showing his contempt
Eumenes is baffled and cannot find the reason
he rushes into battle at once, into the trap Hannibal has set

essays.lemma: qui ubi ad naves … fuga salutem petiit
essays.q: how does Nepos make Eumenes look foolish?
points: his side lets an enemy messenger through and takes him straight to the king
everyone assumes the letter must be about peace
the messenger openly gives away the king’s ship to his own side
the letter contains nothing but mockery
Eumenes is puzzled and cannot work out what it means
he still joins battle at once without hesitation
the whole Bithynian fleet attacks his ship and the king has to flee for his life

essays.q: how does Nepos show that Hannibal’s plan worked exactly as he intended?
points: the Bithynians attack Eumenes’ ship all together, just as Hannibal ordered
the king cannot withstand them and flees
he only just escapes to his defences on the shore
the rest of the Pergamene fleet seems to be winning until the pots arrive
the pots are thrown as planned, and at first the enemy laughs
when the snakes appear the Pergamenes panic at the unheard-of attack
unable to decide which danger to avoid, they turn and flee to their camp

essays.q: how does Nepos use this episode to confirm his view of Hannibal as a great general?
points: Rome’s ally Eumenes is reduced to running away
Hannibal’s planning reverses the battle just when the Pergamenes seem to be winning
the enemy is beaten by a weapon nobody could have prepared for
the panic of the Pergamenes shows how completely they are outwitted
Nepos sums up the victory as strategy defeating arms
he widens it into proof that Hannibal often won on land too
prudentia recalls chapter 1, where Hannibal surpassed all other generals in skill

essays.lemma: quae dum in Asia … facile inventuros
essays.q: how does Nepos present the Romans and Prusias in their dealings over Hannibal?
points: the Romans learn where Hannibal is by chance, at a dinner party
Flamininus reports it to the senate the very next day
the senate fears plots as long as Hannibal lives, though he is an old exile
they send envoys, Flamininus among them, to demand that Prusias hand him over
they call Hannibal their bitterest enemy
Prusias is too afraid of Rome to refuse
he hides behind the laws of hospitality while telling the Romans where to find him

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as calm and in control at the end of his life?
points: he had foreseen the danger and built his fortress with exits on every side
when the boy reports armed men, he gives clear, practical orders
he checks whether he is surrounded on all sides
he grasps the situation at once: the Romans are hunting him
he decides calmly that he should not keep his life
he chooses to die on his own terms, at no one else’s will
mindful of his past courage, he takes the poison he always carried

essays.lemma: huc cum legati … anno acquievit septuagesimo
essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s death moving?
points: the great general is trapped in his own house by Roman envoys
the danger is reported by a slave boy at the door
his careful precautions fail: every exit is blocked
he realises that he is being hunted
he chooses death to keep control of his fate, mindful of his past courage
he takes the poison he had always kept with him
Nepos’ final verdict calls him the bravest of men, who found rest after many hardships
